questions.question: What is the definition of offensive language?

result.answer:
A post is labeled offensive (OFF) if it contains any form of non-acceptable language (profanity) or a targeted offense, which can be veiled or direct. [1]
The offensive category includes insults, threats, and posts containing profane language or swear words. [1]
In the OLID dataset, a hierarchical annotation model with three levels is used to distinguish whether language is offensive (A) and the type (B) and target (C) of the offensive language. [2]

questions.question: Is the position in the sequence part of the input?

result.answer:
At every timestep t, the network takes as input an image I_i from the sequence. [1]
In the baseline approach, the encoder takes the sequence of images as input. [2]
In the baseline approach, the decoder takes the last state of the encoder as its first state to generate the story. [3]
Having an independent decoder for each position of the image sequence allowed the visual storyteller to build more specific language models. [4]
Each decoder generates the word sequence for its corresponding image position, allowing each decoder to learn a specific language model for each position of the sequence. [5]
尚待确认：The records do not explicitly state whether the position in the sequence is itself an input to the model; they describe per-position decoders and image inputs, but not a position input.

questions.question: What baseline model is used?

result.answer:
The baseline used is the same baseline as used by lang2011unsupervised, which has been shown to be difficult to outperform. [1]
This baseline assigns a semantic role to a constituent based on its syntactic function, i.e. the dependency relation to its head. [1]
A separate "supervised baseline" was constructed: for predicates seen in the supervised sentences, a MAP estimate of the parameters was calculated using the predefined mapping, and for unseen predicates the standard baseline was used. [2]
Because the CoNLL annotations have 21 semantic roles in total, 21 roles are used in the model as well as the baseline. [3]

questions.question: How does the neural network architecture accomodate an unknown amount of senses per word?

result.answer:
The approach extracts glosses of all N possible senses of each target word from WordNet to form the gloss sentence, with N=4 in the given example. [1]
Context-gloss pairs are constructed from glosses of all possible senses of the target word, treating WSD as a sentence-pair classification problem. [2]

questions.question: Do they incoprorate WordNet into the model?

result.answer:
The paper's own method extracts word sense glosses from WordNet 3.0, because BIBREF17 mapped all sense annotations in these datasets to WordNet 3.0. [1]
The paper describes BIBREF12 as leveraging gloss information from WordNet and modeling the semantic relationship between context and gloss in an improved memory network. [2]
The paper states that prior attempts show incorporating gloss knowledge into supervised WSD is helpful, but they have not achieved much improvement. [3]
尚待确认：The records do not explicitly state whether WordNet itself (as a resource or embedding) is incorporated into the model, beyond extracting glosses from WordNet 3.0.；The records do not specify the exact model architecture or how the extracted glosses are fed into the model.

questions.question: How are the different components of the model trained? Is it trained end-to-end?

result.answer:
The proposed BERT-based natural language generation model can be trained end-to-end without handcrafted features. [1]
BERT is used on both the encoder and decoder of a seq2seq model, with a two-stage decoding structure. [2]
During training, the model's objective is the sum of the two processes, jointly trained using the teacher-forcing algorithm. [3]
During training, the ground-truth summary is fed to each decoder and the objective is minimized. [3]
All of the models are built on BERT_BASE. [4]

documents.title: A Hybrid Architecture for Multi-Party Conversational Systems

questions.question: What is the state of the art described in the paper?

result.answer:
The paper discusses the state of the art on conversational systems from three perspectives: types of interactions, types of architecture, and types of context reasoning. [1]
The paper states that the most recent state of the art for developing such systems has employed Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), Dynamic Context-Sensitive Generation, and Memory Networks, among others. [2]

questions.question: How did they extend LAMA evaluation framework to focus on negation?

result.answer:
The negated LAMA dataset was constructed by inserting negation elements (e.g., “not”) into LAMA cloze statements. [1]
The work questions the extent to which factual knowledge in negated statements is indirectly acquired during pretraining. [2]
The work shows that pretrained language models have problems handling negation. [3]
Negation is examined using a dataset of 72 simple sentences querying for category membership. [4]
In a case study, they test for correct licensing environments for negative polarity items. [5]
They study a set of classifiers distinguishing between grammatically correct and incorrect sentences. [6]

questions.question: What word level and character level model baselines are used?

result.answer:
The character-level model has 1.2M parameters, while the word-level model has 19.9M parameters. [1]
The word-level model achieves a best SQ accuracy of 53.9%. [1]
Both word-level and character-level models reach around 80% accuracy when predicting the predicate. [2]
The word-level model predicts only 45% of entities accurately from the mixed set. [2]
Character-level modeling is used to handle the OOV issue, in contrast to word-level modeling. [3]
The character-level encoder-decoder framework improves performance over state-of-the-art word-level neural models and is more compact. [4]
The OOV issue is more severe for the word-level model because no data augmentation is used to cover entities unseen in the train set. [5]
Word-level models were explored as an alternative to character-level models for constructing embeddings for questions, entities and predicates. [6]

questions.question: How are the supervised scores of the words calculated?

result.answer:
The neural network that learns word embeddings is built using contextual information about the data and supervised scores of the words. [1]
The work captures the supervised information by utilising emoticons as features. [1]
For words occurring in the same contexts as the target word, minimum, maximum, and average polarity scores are taken into consideration. [2]
The word polarity scores are computed using (DISPLAY_FORM4). [2][3]
Three hand-crafted polarity scores—minimum, mean, and maximum—are extracted from each review. [3]
These three scores are concatenated to the averaged word vector per review. [4]
尚待确认：The records do not state the actual formula behind (DISPLAY_FORM4), so the exact calculation of the supervised/polarity scores cannot be determined.；The records do not explicitly define the term "supervised scores" as identical to the polarity scores; that correspondence is not confirmed.

result.answer:
The Turkish movie corpus was used as the first dataset and consists of movie reviews collected from a popular website. [1]
The movie corpus contains 20,244 reviews, with an average of 39 words per review. [1]
Using SVM to predict review labels, the authors achieved accuracies of over 90 per cent for the Turkish movie corpus. [2]
Success rates for the movie corpus were much better than those for the Twitter dataset for most approaches, because tweets are generally much shorter and noisier. [3]
The TDK dictionary covers most of the domain-specific vocabulary used in the movie reviews, so the dictionary method performs well. [4]
The Twitter corpus, described as the second Turkish dataset, consists of tweets about Turkish mobile network operators that are mostly much noisier and shorter than the reviews in the movie corpus. [5]

questions.question: what was the baseline?

result.answer:
The model first quickly learns to copy baseline translations, and the BLEU score with the baseline is very high at that stage. [1]
As the model gradually learns to change the baseline translations, BLEU with the reference translation improves while BLEU with the baseline drops. [1]
DocRepair outperforms the baseline and CADec by 0.7 BLEU. [2]
Annotators showed a strong preference for corrected translations over the baseline ones. [3]
For the evaluation, only examples where a DocRepair translation was not a full copy of the baseline one were picked. [4]

questions.question: What is the goal of investigating NLP gender bias specifically in the news broadcast domain and Anchor role?

result.answer:
The paper introduces the notion of speaker's role to refine its analysis of gender representation in terms of voice professionalism. [1]
The investigation concerns the impact of speaker's gender and role on performance, with WER computed for each speaker at the episode level. [2]
Speaker's role appears to affect WER, with an average WER of 30.8% for Anchor speakers versus 42.23% for Punctual speakers. [3]
No significant gender bias is observed within the Anchor category. [4]
Gender bias varies across speaker's role and speech spontaneity level, with WER increases of 27.2% for Punctual speakers and 31.8% for spontaneous speech between male and female speakers. [5]

questions.question: What extracted features were most influencial on performance?

result.answer:
The record states that gains in performance were demonstrated due to the features, ensemble schemes, multi-tasking and multi-granularity architectures, but it does not rank which extracted features were most influential. [1]
Linguistic features were used in a multi-task LSTM-CRF sequence tagger designed to jointly detect propagandistic fragments and their type. [2]
Linguistic, layout and topical features were investigated in two binary classifiers, LogisticRegression and CNN. [3]
Adding BERTSentEmb to the multi-grained LSTM-CRF improved scores on dev (internal) but not on dev (external). [4]
尚待确认：The records do not identify which specific extracted features were most influential on performance or provide a feature-level ranking or comparison.；The records do not provide per-feature performance metrics or ablation results isolating individual extracted features.

questions.question: How is the vocabulary of word-like or phoneme-like units automatically discovered?

result.answer:
Raw acoustic feature-based unsupervised term discovery (UTD) aims to identify and cluster repeating word-like units across speech based around segmental dynamic time warping (DTW). [1]
A model-based alternative for producing speech tokenizations without language dependency is unsupervised learning of hidden Markov model (HMM) based phoneme-like units from untranscribed speech. [2]
After tokenizations are obtained by either UTD or AUD, each spoken document is represented by a vector of unigram occurrence counts over discovered terms, or a vector of n-gram counts over acoustic units, respectively. [3]
The paper states three questions worth investigating in its AUD-based setting, including whether a CNN-based framework can perform as well on noisy automatically discovered phoneme-like units as on orthographic words/characters. [4]

result.answer:
In the recorded experiments, the authors observed that some outputs preferred to repeat the same word, as shown in Table TABREF38. [1]
The recorded explanation for the repetition is that reinforcement learning rewards encourage the model to generate words that get high scores from classifiers, and back-translation cannot stop it. [1]
The authors also report encountering the "No Change" issue during their experiments, where style transfer models such as DualRL tend to make few changes and output the same sentence. [2]

questions.question: What are the difficulties in modelling the ironic pattern?

result.answer:
A recorded difficulty is that many non-ironic sentences lack specific stylistic words, making it difficult in practice to transfer non-ironic sentences to ironic sentences through the content/style separation approach. [1][2]
Because the goal is to transfer sentences from non-ironic to ironic, the record states that using only one classifier is not enough, so two pre-trained sentiment classifiers are implemented for non-ironic and ironic sentences respectively. [3]
The model's goal is to generate an ironic sentence from a non-ironic sentence while preserving the content and sentiment polarity of the source input sentence. [4]

The study focuses on the answerability of questions on Quora, i.e., whether a posted question eventually gets answered. [1]
The records include a Quora example question about advances in treatment of traumatic brain injuries, posted 23 June 2011 and first answered 22 April 2013. [2]
The records also mention related work analyzing and predicting unanswered questions on Yahoo Answers. [3]

documents.title: Pre-trained Language Model Representations for Language Generation

questions.question: What language model architectures are used?

result.answer:
The work considers two types of architectures: a bi-directional language model to augment the sequence-to-sequence encoder and a uni-directional model to augment the decoder. [1]
Pre-trained representations from language models are applied to language generation tasks modeled by sequence-to-sequence architectures. [2]
The ELMo module forms a linear combination of the language model layers using learned scalar parameters and also considers the input word embeddings of the language model. [3]
The same strategy is applied to the decoder: language model representations are input to the decoder network and the language model is fine-tuned when training the sequence-to-sequence model. [4]

questions.question: What dataset do they use?

result.answer:
Most experiments use the WMT'18 English-German (en-de) news translation task, with findings validated on the WMT'18 English-Turkish (en-tr) news task. [1]
For WMT'18 English-German, the training corpus is all available bitext excluding ParaCrawl, with sentences longer than 250 tokens and sentence-pairs with a source/target length ratio exceeding 1.5 removed, resulting in 5.18M sentence pairs. [2]
For WMT'18 English-Turkish, all available bitext comprising 208K sentence-pairs is used without any filtering. [3]
For the WMT'18 English-Turkish task, the language model vocab is used for the English side of the bitext and a BPE vocabulary learned on the Turkish side. [4]
The work also considers an abstractive document summarization task comprising over 280K news articles paired with multi-sentence summaries. [5]

questions.question: What is the attention module pretrained on?

result.answer:
Previous work BIBREF6 trains attention modules separately for ASR, MT and ST, so the ST attention module does not benefit from pre-training. [1]
The proposed TCEN approach pre-trains the attention module. [2]
The pre-trained MT attention module is reused in ST to leverage alignment information learned in pre-training. [3]
尚待确认：The records do not explicitly state the dataset or task on which the attention module itself is pre-trained; they only indicate that the MT attention module is pre-trained and reused in ST.

questions.question: What topics are included in the debate data?

result.answer:
The CreateDebate dataset was collected from an English online debate forum discussing four topics: abortion (ABO), gay rights (GAY), Obama (OBA), and marijuana (MAR). [1]
For the FBFans dataset, the only general known topic is nuclear power plants; the LDA topic model was applied to determine latent topics. [2]
